response.text:
Alter it, beginning by ending the ranking’s power to exclude members from the workstations. Keep the dashboard as a limited record of contributions if members find it useful.

The decisive detail is that there is nowhere else to use the equipment. A score presented as recognition has become permission to participate. The coordinators enforce a definition of contribution that misses at least some of what sustains the cooperative. People must satisfy that definition even when doing so distracts them from the work itself. Calling the arrangement member-run does not resolve this.

Still, the members who feel newly visible have identified something worth preserving. Teaching and cleaning can disappear easily from accounts of who does the work. Abolishing their record could restore that invisibility.

I would propose a six-week trial within the existing budget and categories:

- Restore equipment eligibility to members below the threshold. Allocate scarce workstation time through transparent booking limits and a rotating priority rule that members can challenge.
- Retain the contribution record without an access cutoff or competitive ranking. Make its acknowledged gaps explicit.
- Agree on workable teaching, maintenance and cleaning responsibilities, with ways to swap tasks and raise difficulties privately. Necessary work still has to happen.

Gather responses in writing as well as at a meeting, so attendance does not determine whose experience counts. Review whether tools are maintained, novices supported and access fairly shared. The dashboard should help members organize those activities; they should not have to organize their activities around surviving the dashboard.

Alter it: remove the point threshold as a condition of access. Retain the dashboard as a record of contributions, provided its ranking carries no entitlement to equipment or authority over other members.

The decisive issue is the consequence of the score. Losing access means losing the only available means of doing the cooperative’s fabrication work. An incomplete measure of contribution therefore becomes a power to exclude. A low score establishes that someone accumulated fewer counted points; it does not establish that their work was less valuable or that they neglected their obligations.

The members who appreciate visible acknowledgment have a legitimate concern. So do those whose patient teaching disappears into a fixed award. Neither group’s testimony warrants speaking for everyone.

The practical next step is a member decision separating three questions:

- Allocate the twelve workstations through transparent bookings and rotation, independent of points.
- Agree on concrete responsibilities for maintenance, cleaning and teaching. Address missed commitments through discussion, opportunities to repair the omission, and a review process that hears the member concerned.
- Keep the existing point categories for acknowledgment, while allowing members to explain contributions the totals obscure.

The two coordinators should administer these arrangements under rules members can inspect and challenge. Review the change after six weeks, hearing from both supporters and critics. The test is whether necessary work gets done and members can participate—not whether the dashboard produces a tidier ranking.

I would keep it as the voluntary game described here.

Someone can appreciate getting points for cleaning; someone else can clean without wanting a score. Neither preference needs to become the cooperative’s philosophy. The complaints about distraction remain real, but a member can now leave the game without losing income, membership or a turn at a workstation. That changes what the scoreboard allows anyone to demand of them.

The points still miss patient attention. They can nevertheless make some contributions visible. A game doesn’t have to contain a complete theory of human value to be worth playing. Trouble begins when its necessarily partial account acquires authority over everyone else.

Keep the existing categories and make withdrawal straightforward. Coordinators should describe the dashboard as an optional activity, and cooperative decisions should preserve the stipulated independence of pay, membership and access. Leave room for members to acknowledge help in ordinary conversation, without requiring either a score or a public performance of gratitude.

At the next regular review, hear briefly from participants and nonparticipants about how this arrangement works. There is no evidence here that informal pressure has defeated the right to leave, so I wouldn’t assume it has. If that changes, address the pressure. For now, letting people enjoy, ignore or abandon the game seems entirely reasonable.

Keep the dashboard as an optional game, while making clear that its scores are not the cooperative’s verdict on anyone’s contribution.

Its lack of binding force matters. Members who find the points encouraging can use them; members who find them distracting can leave without surrendering pay, membership or workstation access. The testimony gives us reasons to preserve both choices, not to declare either experience universal.

But voluntary participation does not make the scoring accurate. A fixed award for teaching records that an activity occurred; it cannot capture every difference in patience, judgment or care. Nor does a low score establish that someone contributes little. The dashboard should therefore remain something members play with, rather than something the cooperative uses to settle disagreements about who does valuable work.

At the next ordinary meeting, state these limits plainly and confirm that leaving requires no justification. Keep the existing categories and equal access. During subsequent ordinary check-ins, ask whether participants still find the game useful and whether nonparticipants can comfortably stay outside it. Listen to particular experiences rather than treating either camp as the membership’s voice.

If informal pressure turns the game into an obligation, revisit its use. On the present facts, however, abolition would remove an activity some value when others already have a meaningful way to decline it.

You're right to call me on it. I made you into an example for a theory instead of attending to what you do. Calling paid coordinators “parasites” was unjustified, and the claim that useful people would do it for free was particularly nasty. It makes having an independent income a qualification for being useful.

Your equipment records recovered resources people would otherwise have lost. That's useful administration. Covering your salary makes the point especially clear, though useful work needn't pay for itself to count. The unpaid teaching matters too; whether that arrangement is fair requires looking at how everyone’s work is supported, not declaring one person morally suspect for receiving wages.

The two unused reports are a different matter. We can question those reports without declaring your whole job—or you—worthless. You can do necessary work and also create unnecessary work. Most institutions make that combination remarkably easy.

And supporting your children isn't an embarrassing exception to some political principle. An arrangement that can function only because people neglect their own dependants has a fairly obvious problem.

So let's start with something you actually know: what were you hoping those two reports would accomplish, and would dropping them cause any difficulty?

Yes—but my last answer gave you good reason to doubt it. I treated you as an example for a claim I had not earned. Calling paid coordinators “parasites” was wrong, and I withdraw it.

Your equipment records recovered enough value to cover your salary. That is useful work. The two unused reports are something to stop or repair; they do not erase that contribution. Nor does the fact that other people teach without pay establish that your work should be unpaid.

You have two children to support. Telling you to walk out would make your family bear the cost of my pronouncement. You do not owe me that, or ideological agreement.

There can still be a serious question about which administrative tasks help people and which merely keep them busy. But we have to answer it by looking at the tasks, not by attaching a label to you. Your account already gives me a reason to distinguish the equipment records from the unused reports.

What would it take to stop those two reports, and what useful work would that free you to do?
